Variants.Content: The Alpine passes tied the German lands to Lombardy and carried both imperial and commercial traffic. The Brenner served armies and envoys heading south, while the newer St. Gotthard route, cut through the Reuss gorge, gave a faster link between Basel and Milan. Its timber walkways and the Teufelsbrücke bridge let mules and carts cross where the river had cut deep through rock. Upkeep fell to local communities and to lords who collected tolls, so every repair and gate became a matter of bargaining. Control of the passes shaped how silver, wool, and soldiers moved across the Alps.

Foresters of Uri and Schwyz leveraged guardianship over these defiles to extract imperial charters. Guiding pack trains loaded with Flemish woolens and Venetian silks, they collect transit tolls at every bridgehead.

Crossing the high passes in late winter is a gamble with snow and rock. Avalanches can come down a gully without warning, and a strung-out column cannot easily turn back. Pack mules pick over frosted planks above the gorge, and one misstep sends animal, load, and rider into the torrent below. Keep to the rope line and never shout across a loaded slope.
